stem: Reformers supported the Dawes Act as a humane way to help Native peoples, yet it left them poorer. What best explains that outcome?

stimulus.source_note: Dawes Severalty Act, Feb. 8, 1887, 24 Stat. 388, Sec. 1. Public domain. Text verified against the Statutes at Large via govinfo (STATUTE-24-Pg388) and EBSCO's document analysis of the act's provisions.
stimulus.text:
Dawes Severalty Act (General Allotment Act) of 1887, Section 1 (ellipses mark omissions):

"That in all cases where any tribe or band of Indians has been, or shall hereafter be, located upon any reservation created for their use... the President of the United States be, and he hereby is, authorized... to allot the lands in said reservation in severalty to any Indian located thereon in quantities as follows:"

"To each head of a family, one-quarter of a section; To each single person over eighteen years of age, one-eighth of a section; To each orphan child under eighteen years of age, one-eighth of a section; and To each other single person under eighteen years now living... one-sixteenth of a section..."

(Paraphrase of Section 5: the United States would hold each allotment in trust for twenty-five years, after which the owner would receive title and citizenship.)

options.text: The act gave Native peoples too much land, which they could not farm
options.misconception: Background: the allotments were 160 acres at most, and much of the land was arid; the problem was too little usable land, not too much.

options.text: The act was never passed by Congress and never took effect
options.misconception: Background: Congress passed the act in 1887 and it operated for decades; its effects are the story, not its failure to pass.

options.text: The act returned all reservation land to tribal ownership
options.misconception: Background: the act did the opposite of returning land; it divided tribal land into individual plots and sold what was left over.

options.text: Allotment broke up tribal lands and left farms too small and dry to work

rationales.A: Background: 160 acres was the largest share, and on the dry Plains it was too little for farming or grazing. The act starved its farmers, it did not drown them in land.
rationales.B: Background: the act passed in 1887 and ran for nearly fifty years, until the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 reversed it.
rationales.C: Background: the act dissolved tribal ownership into individual allotments and sold the leftover, or surplus, land to white settlers.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the reformers' plan was assimilation through private property, but the allotments were small and dry, the surplus was sold off, and Native landholdings fell from about 138 million acres in 1887 to about 48 million by 1934.
rationales.general:
A good intention can still be a disaster, so measure the law by its acres, not its motives.
1. Take the reformers' hope: private farms would make Native peoples self-sufficient citizens.
2. Measure the land. Background: 160 dry acres could not support a Plains farm, and the surplus went to settlers.
3. Count the result. Background: two-thirds of the tribal land base vanished in a generation.
Remember: judge a policy by what happened to the people, not by what its friends hoped.
